item.title: How to Recognise Coercive Narrative
item.description:
Cognition

How to Recognise Coercive Narrative

Recognizing the array of narrative controlling devices will support our open minds.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Coercive narrative manipulates others into accepting a dominant story.
  • Devices for enforcing narrative control often go unnoticed.
  • Coercive narrative devices include styles of delivery, threatening rebuttals, and conversation closers.

Gaslighting, whereby someone undermines our belief in our own experiences, is now a familiar term, while other hurdles to personal knowledge have been overlooked. One of these is coercive narrative, whereby devices are used to ensure we accept a dominant version of a person and their motives or of events and their causes.

In the past decade or so, I, like many others, have become increasingly sensitive to ways our own stories about what is happening in our lives are drowned out by loud narratives—not because they are lyrically persuasive or convincing but because they hedge their position with silencers or signals that of disapproval and contempt and confusion. Coercive narrative is not simply a fixed personal belief; it inflicts a fixed story on others. The "story" can be specific—about an individual person or event or process—or it can be more general about how the world "really" is or works.

One way to resist controlling narratives is to identify common techniques used to enforce them.

Delivery Style

First, we can spot delivery techniques that secure speech time through body language as well as voice. By refusing to look at people to whom you are speaking, you avoid signaling that it is their turn to speak. A stiff chest and shoulders convey determination not to be moved, though the very different posture of appearing to relax your shoulders while spreading your arms (and sometimes lifting one ankle to rest across the other leg’s thigh) signal great comfort and confidence in your position while also showing entitlement to more space.

Vocal ploys to support body language include speaking continuously (often quickly) and loudly, filling any lapse in flow with fillers such as "uhhh" to indicate that even though you may have run out of vocal steam, you still own the verbal platform.

Rebuttals

Next come preemptive dismissals of possible alternative views. "Anyone who does not agree with me is stupid or ignorant or a bad actor." Or "I’ve had enough of experts; their views are worthless." In a more personal context, we might be told, "She’ll tell you I’m abusive, but everyone knows she’s a liar." Or "He’s too limited to understand this/know what’s really going on."

Dire predictions can also be used to coerce narratives: "This is all going to fall apart if you don’t see it my way," or, "If I hadn’t acted, this land would be destroyed/this family would collapse/you wouldn’t be alive." These are often accompanied by confident positive predictions: "You will soon thank me/be so glad you listened…"

The kitchen-sink approach is used when others persist in dissent. Arguments in support of the controlling narrative come thick and fast. Whether or not the arguments and examples are relevant (or accurate), the barrage of "reasoning" disorients others so they lose track of where to start with a counterargument.

article continues after advertisement

Distorted agreement is a technique used in cases where the coercer is required to hear the other’s point of view (because of their position and status). The coercer might appear to agree with what’s said but then repeat it with a twist that pulls it within their box. "What you’re really saying is that we need clarity, and that’s what my story provides," or "What I hear you saying is that we have to go forward in this way."

Pat answers squash hesitancy in accepting the narrative: "That [whatever you’re worried about] won’t happen," or "I know why you think that, but it doesn’t apply here," or "Lots of people think that, but they don’t understand how things work."

Pat explanations undermine any evidence against the coercer’s narrative: "It only seems that way because you’re not given all the facts," or "Of course that’s what he would say."

Mocking dismissal such as "You don’t really believe that/You can’t be that stupid/You’re too smart not to see…" boxes the audience into a corner where dissent is difficult.

Closing the Narrative

Finally, the lid on the boxed story needs to be snapped shut. The coercer might do this with a general platitude such as, "What I’m saying is, don’t try to fix what isn’t broken," or "An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, so we have to act now," or "We have to strike while the iron’s hot." Shifting argument from a specific issue to a very general precept makes it difficult to formulate objections.

Self-boosting epithets might be offered to reassure you that the boxed-up story has a good pedigree: "I’m the kind of person who sees things as they are/calls a spade a spade/doesn’t waste time."

Narrative coercion by politicians stifles public discussion. When used by a parent, it limits a child from articulating and even formulating their individual experiences. When used by a spouse, it minimizes the partner’s influence on children, finances, and daily routines. We are better equipped to protect ourselves when we can spot the devices used to box us into the coerced narrative.

item.title: Why Losing a Child Shatters the World
item.description:
Grief

Why Losing a Child Shatters the World

A child’s death can wound six universal psychological needs at once.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • A child’s death can disrupt identity, attachment, agency, dignity, and meaning at once.
  • Prolonged grief is not weak mourning; it is a treatable breakdown in adaptation.
  • Healing preserves the bond while gradually restoring a life worth living.

A couple sat across from me, both dressed in dark clothing and speaking quietly. Two years earlier, their young adult daughter had died in a bus accident while studying abroad. “When the police came to our door, everything collapsed,” the mother said. “Since then, I have known no joy. Life has no value anymore.” She could not bear words associated with death or burial and thought about her daughter “24/7.”

Her husband began to cry. “She was our angel,” he said. “It still hurts in my soul. But we have three younger children. I have to work. I have to function.” The couple barely spoke. The mother frequently stopped him when he mentioned the loss: “You do not have my pain.”

This composite vignette reflects recurring clinical patterns; identifying details have been changed.

For more than two decades, I have studied parental responses to a child’s death. Classic life-event research placed bereavement among the experiences requiring the greatest psychological readjustment. Recent reviews show that parental bereavement can disrupt identity, relationships, health, spirituality, social belonging, and the anticipated future. A meta-analysis of 120 studies involving 61,580 adults identified child or partner loss, unexpected or unnatural death, and pre-existing depression among the risks for prolonged grief symptoms. Fathers may express grief more instrumentally, through work, responsibility, or silence, without suffering less.

Why This Loss Reaches So Deeply

A child is woven into a parent’s identity, responsibilities, family structure, and imagined future. Parents ordinarily expect to protect their children and to die before them. A child’s death reverses this assumed order and removes both a present relationship and a future that had become psychologically real.

The Theory of Universal Psychological Needs (TUPG) identifies six universal needs: safety/predictability, attachment/belonging, autonomy/influence, competence/effectiveness, dignity/recognition, and meaning/coherence. A child’s death can injure all six at once.

  1. Safety and predictability collapse. A sudden accident can destroy the assumption that life is sufficiently orderly and loved ones will return home.
  2. Attachment and belonging are torn apart. Continuous preoccupation may partly function as an attempt to prevent a second loss—the loss of the inner relationship.
  3. Autonomy and influence are defeated. Parents are organized around protecting and helping their children. “If only I had…” thoughts create an imagined possibility of control while deepening guilt.
  4. Competence and effectiveness are shaken. Even without objective responsibility, parents may feel they failed in their most fundamental role. Work, caregiving, and everyday decisions can then appear pointless.
  5. Dignity and recognition are threatened. Bereaved parents may feel that no one understands their pain. Pressure to “move on” can feel like a denial of both the child and their continuing identity as a parent.
  6. Meaning and coherence may disintegrate. The question becomes not only “Why did this happen?” but “What kind of world—or God—could allow it?” The future may feel wrong because the child was denied one.
article continues after advertisement

These injuries interact. Withdrawal may initially reduce triggers and protect the bond. Over time, however, it also removes experiences of belonging, influence, competence, recognition, and meaning. A strategy that reduces pain today may maintain suffering tomorrow.

When Grief Becomes Entrapping

Enduring love and sadness are not disorders, and grief has no universal timetable. Cultural and religious contexts matter. But when preoccupation dominates nearly every day, functioning remains severely impaired, the future is rejected, and life feels worthless, prolonged grief disorder and depression require professional assessment.

Different grieving styles can also create relational injury. One parent may talk and cry; another may work, organize, or remain silent. Neither response proves greater love. Problems arise when one partner’s grief invalidates the other’s, or surviving children learn that joy is forbidden. Reviews emphasize the need to support parents and siblings, while also showing that evidence for whole-family interventions remains limited.

Healing Does Not Mean Letting Go

The goal is not to detach from the child or replace grief with positive thinking. Worden’s widely used tasks-of-mourning framework describes adaptation as recognizing the loss, processing its pain, adjusting to a changed world, and finding an enduring connection with the deceased while continuing life. TUPG adds a systematic question: Which needs have been injured, and how can each be restored?

First, safety comes before meaning. Statements such as “Life has no value” require direct assessment of suicidal thoughts, plans, access to means, and the person’s ability to remain safe. Severe depression may require psychiatric care alongside psychotherapy.

Second, treatment should address grief specifically. A 2024 meta-analysis of 22 studies involving 2,602 adults found that grief-focused cognitive behavioral therapies reduced prolonged grief symptoms and also improved depression, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress symptoms. Treatment may include gradually approaching avoided memories, processing the death, examining guilt and responsibility, and rebuilding activities and relationships.

Third, the child’s life must become larger than the child’s death. Therapy can help parents recover memories of the child’s voice, humor, values, relationships, and hopes, so traumatic images no longer occupy the entire biography.

Fourth, the couple needs room for two legitimate forms of grief. Each partner should be able to speak without interruption or comparison. Surviving children need honest, age-appropriate communication, stable routines, emotional availability, and explicit permission to experience both grief and joy.

article continues after advertisement

Recovery is rarely a return to the former self. It is the gradual restoration of psychological regulation: a little more safety, one reliable relationship, one self-chosen action, one experience of effectiveness, one moment of being understood, and eventually one reason to face tomorrow.

Continuing to live does not mean leaving the child behind. It means finding a way for the child to remain part of one’s life without requiring the rest of the family to stop living too.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: What Is Your Psychological Footprint?
item.description:
Resilience

What Is Your Psychological Footprint?

The lasting impact of your thoughts, emotions, and behaviors.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • The person we become is largely shaped by the patterns we repeatedly practice.
  • We cannot control every circumstance, but we can control how we respond to those circumstances.
  • The path to greater well-being begins when we stop arguing with reality and start working with it.
Source: Free Adobe stock by Tamara Sales

This is the profound, simple truth: You are the master of your life and death. What you do is what you are. —Hua Hu Ching

Most people are familiar with the idea of a carbon footprint—the impact our daily choices have on the environment. But there is another footprint we leave behind every day, one that may be even more consequential: our psychological footprint.

Your psychological footprint is the lasting impact of your thoughts, emotions, attitudes, and behaviors on yourself and the people around you. It is the emotional residue you leave in your relationships, the habits you reinforce in your mind, and the patterns that shape your experience of life.

Ancient traditions called this karma. While karma is often misunderstood as cosmic reward and punishment, its original meaning is much simpler: action.

From a psychological perspective, karma can be understood as the cumulative effects of our choices. Every action, thought, and reaction strengthens certain neural pathways, influences our relationships, and shapes the person we become. The more we repeat a behavior, the more automatic it becomes. In this way, our future is influenced not by fate but by the habits we practice today.

Philosopher Alan Watts captured this idea when he observed that life is not a “whodunit” but a “you-dunit.” While we cannot control every circumstance that comes our way, we contribute to the quality of our experience through how we respond to those circumstances.

Modern psychology supports this view. Research on habit formation, emotional intelligence, and neuroplasticity suggests that our daily thoughts and behaviors create patterns that influence our well-being. Optimism tends to strengthen resilience. Gratitude promotes psychological health. Chronic resentment and negativity, on the other hand, often reinforce stress and emotional suffering.

Yet many of us move through life on autopilot. We react rather than respond. We repeat the same emotional habits without questioning them. Over time, we may find ourselves wondering why we keep encountering the same frustrations, conflicts, or disappointments.

Often, what feels like bad luck is actually the accumulation of unnoticed patterns. We blame circumstances, other people, or fate without recognizing our role in shaping the outcome. This is not about self-blame. Rather, it is about reclaiming personal agency.

article continues after advertisement

One of the most powerful ways to improve our psychological footprint is through acceptance. Acceptance does not mean approval or resignation. It means acknowledging reality as it is rather than exhausting ourselves fighting against it. Much of our emotional suffering comes not from events themselves but from our resistance to them.

When we stop arguing with reality, we free up psychological energy that can be redirected toward growth, meaning, and purposeful action.

Ultimately, understanding your psychological footprint means becoming mindful of how you invest your attention, emotions, and energy. The following practices can help create a healthier footprint for yourself and those around you.

1. Conserve Your Emotional Energy

Pay attention to what drains you. Chronic worry, people-pleasing, unresolved conflict, and perfectionism can consume enormous amounts of psychological energy. Learn where your energy goes and whether the return is worth the investment.

2. Recharge Intentionally

Just as your phone needs charging, so does your mind. Spend time engaged in activities that promote positive emotions and restore resilience. Recharge your creativity, meaningful relationships, exercise, spirituality, humor, or simple moments of reflection.

article continues after advertisement

3. Practice Strategic Stillness

In a culture that glorifies busyness, rest can feel unproductive. Yet psychological research consistently demonstrates that periods of rest, mindfulness, and solitude improve emotional regulation, decision-making, and overall well-being.

4. Expand Your Sources of Wisdom

Psychological flexibility is one of the strongest predictors of mental health. Remain open to new ideas, different perspectives, and opportunities for growth. Wisdom can be found in science, philosophy, spirituality, literature, and lived experience.

5. Remember That You Are Connected

Human beings are relational creatures. Our moods, behaviors, and attitudes influence those around us more than we realize. Every interaction leaves a trace. Ask yourself: What emotional footprint am I leaving behind today?

In the end, your psychological footprint is not measured by what happens to you but by how you respond to what life brings your way. Every thought you nurture, every habit you practice, and every interaction you have contributes to the person you are becoming.

The good news is that your footprint is not fixed. Each day offers a new opportunity to create one that reflects greater awareness, compassion, resilience, and purpose.

item.title: Stage Fright and the Heroic Struggle of Being
item.description:
Stage Fright

Stage Fright and the Heroic Struggle of Being

An existential-phenomenological approach to stage fright.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Musical performance anxiety can be reframed as a meaningful part of the human condition and lived experience.
  • We may confront core existential pillars—freedom, isolation, meaning, and finitude—on the high-stakes stage.
  • We can embrace struggle through will to power to forge authentic self-fulfillment rather than seek perfection.

Whereas traditional psychology often views music performance anxiety (MPA) as a set of symptoms, a biologically “hardwired” evolutionary reaction, or the consequence of cognitive distortions, the existential-phenomenological psychologist understands MPA as a subjective, meaningfully inherent aspect of the human condition. Rather than a disorder to be cured, stage fright is viewed as a part of the experiential whole of performing for others.

In phenomenology, we explore and dwell within the subjective “lived experience” of performing music. This does not only include the rewarding aspects of joy that come from sharing music in a public setting, but also the difficult aspects of anxiety, worry, and fear. Fully embracing the raw experience of public performance in its entirety, and embracing both the joyous and difficult aspects of public performance, offers us an appreciation of the rich, textured, and complex realities of public performance.

Public performance brings both bliss and fear that we can experience as a shift in the experience of time. The temporality of our lived experience can feel like it is slowing down with anticipation, or speeding up with loss of control. This state of fluid temporality can feel disorienting and fearful. It can also bring us feelings of freedom and bliss.

We can also experience anticipatory dread that comes from a hyper-reflexive awareness of ourselves as performers. Motions that are typically second nature seem foreign and awkward under the hyper-reflexive lens of self-consciousness that occurs when we are on public display. Understanding that we have volitionally chosen to be in this situation adds another dimension of existential consideration to the situation. In many ways, we are choosing to place ourselves in a situation that creates extreme discomfort and extreme joy. In the case of children being forced by a parent or teacher to participate in public performance, the dread is not one volitional choice, but rather a reaction to the loss of autonomy and free choice by being forced into the public performance.

For many musicians, the subjective experience of the public performance can create a feeling of dread and conflict with one’s instrument and one’s body. The loss of control over breathing, physical trembling, and the intrusive thoughts of worry can feel like our body and mind are betraying us. The lack of responsiveness from our instrument can feel like it has become our opponent or our enemy.

4 Core Pillars of Existential Theory

Exploring and contemplating the phenomenological, lived experience of pubic performance can help familiarize ourselves with what is happening when we experience MPA. Existential concerns can help us to understand how these experiences are taking place.

Freedom is a core pillar of existential theory. During a public performance, we are brought into direct contact with both freedom and responsibility—on public display. Complete freedom is terrifying. We experience angst and dread while facing it in this concentrated form. This is both exhilarating and terrifying. Freedom is a defining aspect of our identity and sense of self. When confronted with the angst of complete freedom on public display, we are risking our sense of identity, our understanding of selfhood.

By placing ourselves on the stage, we are separating ourselves from the group and inviting them to scrutinize our performance and our value. It is a sort of question asked. There is a complicated dynamic that comes from the presence of the audience and the performer. This exacerbates another pillar of existentialism, which is isolation. We have artificially enhanced the reality of being isolated in a world of others. On the stage, we are brought into direct contact with the raw experience of isolation and autonomy.

Meaning and purpose are another pillar of existential thought. As we build up an identity through purpose and meaning, as musicians, we place this identity on display for judgment through the public performance. The risk here is enormous for our sense of identity and the notion we hold of who we are. The public performance can be a test of our sense of identity and meaning.

Finally, existentialism considers the pillar of mortality, finitude. In the public performance, we are placing ourselves in an artificially constructed “judgment day.” A public performance creates a stage in which we must confront our limitations and come to terms with our personal potentialities in a concrete way.

Striving Toward Self-Fulfillment

The existential-phenomenological lens reveals a difficult and dark picture of public performance and the human condition. How then, do we understand the impulse or desire to place ourselves in this situation? The answer comes in the form of a human desire to overcome, to express, and to triumph in the hero’s journey. The philosopher Baruch Spinoza described this as conatus. We can understand it as a striving toward fulfillment, a triumph of the will. Friedrich Nietzsche proposed that we must obey our will to power—that is, the striving toward fulfillment of our purpose. The will to power is not about power over others, but rather a willpower that fulfills one’s sense of self. This becomes the key to experiencing and dealing with the dread and fear we call MPA—a purposeful effort to overcome our fears through coming into direct contact with our fears, dreams, and sense of self.

How then, does one deal with the difficulties of public performance? The existential-phenomenological perspective encourages us to not only encounter, but also to embrace the totality of the public performance experience. Anxiety is not a symptom to overcome but, rather, a reality to live through, with the awareness that it is an essential part of the human condition. We embrace this fear to thrive, to enhance our notion of ourselves, and treat it as an opportunity to forge our sense of self in the fires of struggle. We do not try to escape the discomfort of public performance, but rather, embrace it as an essential aspect of our heroic struggle.

We use the opportunity to shift our focus from hyper-self-awareness and criticism toward that epic endeavor of triumph of the will. A sort of proclamation of “Here I am!” Through this, we cease concerns about perfection and acceptance from others and focus on living to our fullest potential while accepting imperfection and flaws as an essential part of being human, all too human.

For the existential-phenomenological psychologist, public performance and the experience of MPA become a ritual and rite of passage in testing, forging, and realizing the fulfillment of our genuine self.

item.title: 3 Reasons Why Adult Child Blame Can Feel So Jarring
item.description:
Parenting

3 Reasons Why Adult Child Blame Can Feel So Jarring

The emotional toll of adult children blaming their struggles on their parents.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Blame from adult children can challenge not only one's parenting but one's whole identity.
  • Blame reduces a complex history to a single, simplified explanation.
  • Unrelenting blame keeps everyone stuck.

"You ruined my life!"

Few words are more painful for a parent to hear. Even if those exact words never leave your adult child's lips or are never sent via text, many parents hear a close version of the message: "It's your fault that I am struggling." For the many parents (who are, for sure, not perfect) who have spent years living, sacrificing, worrying, and trying their best, the accusation can feel very emotionally overwhelming.

Let's look now at three reasons adult-child blame hits so hard.

1. It Challenges Your Identity, Not Just Your Parenting

As my best friend from kindergarten says, "The only perfect people are in the cemetery." Most parents know they were not perfect. In fact, many parents can list things they wish they had done differently. But when an adult child says, "You ruined my life!" parents really hear it as criticism of a few parenting decisions. They hear it as a judgment of who they are.

This distinction really matters. When your identity feels under attack, it's much harder to stay calm, listen with curiosity, and respond in a balanced, thoughtful way. Instead, like many parents I see in my coaching practice, they find themselves becoming defensive or drowning in guilt.

2. It Reduces a Complex Life Story to a Single Explanation

Parents profoundly influence their children; there is no denying that. But no one person's life is shaped by only one relationship. Genetics, temperament, friendships, teachers, romantic partners, mental health, financial decisions and stress, opportunities, disappointments, and personal choices all play important roles. Blame can feel comforting, because it offers a simple explanation for complicated pain. Unfortunately, simple explanations are often incomplete. When everything is filtered through the belief that "My parents caused all of my problems", it becomes harder to recognize all the other factors that deserve attention.

3. It Keeps Everyone Emotionally Stuck

In my new book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!, I explain how parents can respond when blame becomes the defining feature of the relationship. What I see often is that blame begins as an attempt to make sense of suffering. That's understandable, but healing rarely comes from assigning fault. There's a better way for you as the parent to respond to the blame missiles being fired your way.

Rather than getting wrapped up in guilt, apologizing/rescuing, or defensiveness, I encourage parents to shift the conversation from "Who caused this?" to "What will help us to move forward? That shift doesn't erase the past, but it creates the possibility of reaching their boundaries, greater understanding, and renewed connection. Please hear this doesn't mean minimizing painful childhood experiences, or excusing parents who genuinely caused them. Accountability matters, but so does compassion.

The Takeaway

No parent wants to hear, "You ruined my life". But those words don't have to define the next chapter. When blame is met with curiosity, accountability, and collaborative problem-solving, I have seen that even deeply strained relationships can have a better chance of healing.

item.title: From Gatorade to Addiction and GLP-1s
item.description:
Addiction

From Gatorade to Addiction and GLP-1s

Neuroscience and the gut-brain revolution in obesity and addiction medicine.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Scientific breakthroughs often begin with unexpected observations made while caring for patients.
  • The same reward biology helps explain addiction, binge eating, obesity, and GLP-1 treatment of SUDs.
  • GLP-1 therapies reveal how gut hormones influence reward, craving, and addictive behaviors.

More than 50 years ago, I began my career believing I’d spend my life studying addiction. I never imagined the journey would lead to obesity medicine and compulsive eating—from Gatorade to Ozempic.

Looking back, what surprises me most is not where the science ended up, but how often progress began with unexpected observations made caring for patients. One of my earliest mentors at the University of Florida was the late Robert Cade, M.D., the brilliant nephrologist who invented Gatorade to prevent dehydration in athletes.

Dr. Cade taught me that a scientifically perfect oral rehydration solution accomplishes nothing if people refuse to drink it. After listening to his wife's advice, he added lemon flavoring and later carbohydrates to his electrolyte mixture, making Gatorade useful and palatable. This always reminded me that physiology and behavior are inseparable.

I certainly never imagined that, decades later, gut physiology would become central to my own work through GLP-1 biology. But Cade's lesson stayed with me.

In 1969, Woodstock proved an unexpected natural experiment in competing rewards. Food, music, sex, social connections, and psychoactive drugs all competed for attention. I found myself wondering whether the brain prioritized drugs over natural rewards. I had no way to test that idea, but the question never left me.

During my Yale fellowship in the 1970s, I became immersed in the neurobiology of addiction, studying opioid actions, withdrawal, craving, and compulsive drug use. One of my mentors, Eugene Redmond, M.D., conducted research on the island of St. Kitts. He described watching free-ranging vervet monkeys actively seeking fermented sugar cane and even soft drinks provided by local residents. Because fermented sugar cane naturally contains alcohol, their attraction to both suggested that sugar and alcohol might engage related brain reward processes.

Meanwhile, my patients at Yale taught me equally important lessons. At Herb Kleber's New Haven storefront addiction clinics, cigarette smokers gained weight after quitting. Conversely, cocaine users often forget to eat. Patients withdrawing from opioids developed intense cravings for sweets. During a New Haven blizzard interrupting daily methadone treatment, some patients described eating large amounts of sugar, drinking vodka, or even recreating the ritual of heroin use by heating sugar cubes in spoons to ease withdrawal. Again and again, food and drugs appeared to substitute for one another in remarkably predictable ways.

The opioid, cocaine, and speedball epidemics created another unexpected observation. Residential programs originally designed for alcoholism found many patients developed severe overeating and substantial weight gain after detoxification. Recovery programs soon added nutrition classes, healthier food choices, and treatment for overeating. Clinical experience repeatedly suggested addiction and eating behavior were closely intertwined.

My friend and colleague, Bart Hoebel, at Princeton performed pioneering experiments demonstrating that sugar activates many of the same dopamine circuits engaged by addictive drugs. His laboratory became an ideal place to explore ideas originating in addiction neurobiology and treatment. Those studies grew into my collaborations with Bart and his mentee, Nicole Avena. Elegant animal models showed that intermittent access to sugar could produce behaviors resembling addiction. Highly palatable foods were far more than calories; they engaged many of the same reward systems recruited by cocaine and other drugs of abuse. Later, as Nicole’s mentor on her NIDA K01 Career Development Award examining pharmacotherapies for food addiction, we explored the possibility that some forms of binge eating share important behavioral and neurobiological features with addiction.

Kelly Brownell moved these ideas into mainstream obesity research. We brought together leading addiction scientists and obesity researchers at the Yale Historic Conference on Food and Addiction, challenging us to think differently about overeating. Those discussions ultimately led to our Oxford textbook, Food and Addiction: A Comprehensive Handbook, with 66 chapters written by 100+ experts, helping establish food addiction as a legitimate scientific field.

Another important advance came through Kelly's mentee, Ashley Gearhardt, who helped organize the historic conference and later developed the Yale Food Addiction Scale. For the first time, researchers had a standardized way to study addictive eating behaviors in humans. Our collaborations additionally reinforced the close relationship between smoking, appetite, body weight, and food reward. Smoking suppresses appetite; smoking cessation commonly leads to weight gain, and both nicotine and highly palatable foods engage overlapping motivational circuitry.

My interests gradually expanded into obesity treatment itself. Collaborating with U.F. bariatric surgeons Juan Cendan, M.D., and Robert Rout, M.D., we studied surgical and behavioral interventions, medications including metformin and fenfluramine-phentermine, and gastric stimulation devices. At the time, many surgeons and endocrinologists believed the key to obesity lay primarily in the gut. I believed the answer resided mainly in the brain. I hoped medications developed for addiction—particularly combinations such as bupropion and naltrexone—might also help treat hedonic overeating and binge eating since binge eating shares important behavioral and neurobiological features with addiction, including craving, loss of control, compulsive consumption despite adverse consequences, and relapse.

The eventual FDA approval of the bupropion-naltrexone combination (Contrave) provided one of the first clinical demonstrations that anti-addiction medications acting on reward pathways could also reduce overeating.

But where I was really wrong—and where my obesity colleagues were right—was the importance of the gut-brain pathway.

The Gut Changed the Story

GLP-1s & Translational Addiction Neuroscience
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

I expected addiction neuroscience to transform obesity medicine. Instead, obesity research transformed addiction neuroscience.

Like many addiction researchers, I focused on dopamine, reward, reinforcement, and cortical control. We understood motivation reasonably well but knew comparatively little about the remarkable communication between the gut and the brain. The neurobiology of GLP-1 signaling, hormonal regulation of reward, and dopamine modulation had yet to emerge.

GLP-1 receptor agonists like Ozempic and Mounjaro completed the picture. They revealed that metabolic signals originating in the gut influence neural circuits governing reward, craving, decision-making, and reinforcement. The brain's reward circuitry had always been only one part of a much larger integrated system. Early studies suggest these medications also reduce alcohol consumption and alcohol-related harms, providing further evidence that gut-brain signaling influences reward processes across both overeating and substance use disorders.

Looking back, I no longer think addiction researchers and obesity researchers were studying different diseases. We were studying the same remarkably complex biological system from different directions. Addiction researchers emphasized craving and reinforcement. Eating-disorder researchers focused on binge eating and loss of control. Obesity researchers emphasized appetite and metabolism. Behavioral scientists studied learning. Neuroscientists mapped dopamine circuits. Endocrinologists unraveled gut hormones. Only recently have these perspectives begun to converge.

One lesson has remained constant throughout my career. Scientific progress rarely follows a straight line from laboratory discovery to patient care. More often than not, patients reveal something unexpected. Those observations inspire laboratory experiments. New discoveries lead to better treatments, which generate new clinical questions and send us back to the laboratory. That cycle—from bedside to bench and back again—has defined my career.

I now realize many observations that first appeared unrelated were actually pieces of the same puzzle. Together they revealed a common biology of reward that links addiction, food, obesity, B.E.D., and now GLP-1 therapeutics.

What once seemed like separate fields increasingly look like different windows onto the same biology.

item.title: Expanding Our Sense of Change
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Expanding Our Sense of Change

A Personal Perspective: Preparing for a new understanding of interdependency.

Posted July 21, 2026

"The cosmos is within us. We are made of star-stuff. We are a way for the universe to know itself." —Carl Sagan

"Before the change, there is a prelude, a priming, a saturation of mutual learning between organisms through which pathways of possibility are produced." —Nora Bateson

Expanding Change and Interdependency

What follows is a two-part series; the first half is a story about expanding change and interdependency, and the second is how to be part of this process of change.

Yes, interdependency is commonly defined as characterized by mutual reliance. It is used in the realm of relationships to describe a means to create first-order change that will make an initial difference regarding social/environmental problems. By all accounts, this seems like an excellent framework to create better relationships. Yet we are far from mitigating so many interpersonal difficulties, not to mention environmental and socio-political discord and conflict. How is it that psychotherapy and allopathic medicine, which use interdependency quite often in their goals, for instance, although advanced technology-wise, are still predominantly focused on maintaining the negative effects of poor habitual sustenance, pesticides, and generalized stress? Ivan Illich's concept of iatrogenesis, self-fulfilling illness, is still a prevalent reality in our society.

These outcomes are ill-conceived, fail to account for our complexity, and are treated as separate entities or as needing a specialist. This forces those labeled as change agents, i.e., teachers, medical personnel, and politicians, to become part of the problems, working in isolation. Rather than being allowed to make a difference that makes a difference (a second-order change) in their actions, they are relegated to not creating ongoing, broader change at the overlap and interface with other contexts. Nature, for instance, doesn't depend on fragmentation or opposites. It somehow blends the messiness and beauty of its existence. It is a Ying/Yang lab of changes that redefines interdependency.

Maybe the problem is partly a linguistic issue: not using enough verbs to emphasize our observations and understanding of how each action in our life is constantly being interwoven into nature’s complexity, which cannot always be defined. It is like the adage of the harmonious martial art Aikido that I practiced for 35 years: "you can't hit a moving target," when your actions randomly create changing patterns that manifest as an expansion of our capacity to blend with the ever-changing forces of our environment.

Trees we now know interdepend (the active verb form of interdependency) upon each other in a form of collective communication to preserve and perpetuate their existence. An estuary intermingles its blending potential to send nourishment upstream and downstream simultaneously, with improvisational, randomly balanced results. These processes motivate the ever-changing patterns to adjust as needed to balance our ecosystem. However, our predominant cultural way of perceiving things tends to rely on linear cause-and-effect reasoning that continually separates everything that exists, without considering how it all interdepends on our survival. Profits, unequal distribution of resources, fragmentation of subjects in educational settings, wars, building a road without saving a complex meadow or other living communities, and so on are forms of accelerated entropy resulting from the runaway consequences of real interdependency being interrupted. Hence, the insidious processes of poverty and disaffectedness become a blockage to the many orders of unending change.

Being Part of the Solution

Okay, enough of the obvious insidious patterns. How can we interdepend upon ourselves to have an expanded sense of change and a better use of our interdependency? We can start by using more insightful wisdom about how life coalesces through systemic or ecological action to override the right-or-wrong binaries that dominate our lives. This entails understanding how the whole of a system is more than the sum of its parts. We owe this to our younger generations by sharing, listening, and learning from each other. Change isn't a passive action waiting for you to make it happen; it occurs at every moment. When I began my studies of anthropology, I remember a quote from media theorist Neil Postman asking, "What kinds of changes are going on right now? Which are important?" This includes first-order changes, like recognizing a needed difference, and continuing up to an infinite nth-order change if needed to make a difference.

What I learned from being involved with Nora Bateson's Warm Data Labs is that, as she describes, "ready-ing" is about creating a flexibility alliance for contexts to interface with other contexts through changing interactions. This includes encouraging unseen mutual connection about life's coalescing toward vitality. This process is stimulated by pausing and allowing hypothetical liminal messages to emerge. This leads to recognizing how we can relearn the possibilities of new contexts that will support ongoing changes in non-directional ways. This is the essence of improvisational and stochastic movement that brings us in touch with the ecology of ideas and our interdependency as it is meant to be.

Prompts to Help you Mutually Learn From Each Other

In small groups or side by side with another, especially in intergenerational settings, using win-win dialogue ( volleying by expressing, paraphrasing, checking), allowing for abductive pauses/gaps (hypothetical out-of-the-box insights being in between the prevalent inductive and deductive ways of reasoning), of everyday actions towards expanding change and understanding interdependency:

In what different ways can you encourage flexibility that allows for change within contexts of work, parenting, and family? Media, religion, and schooling? Include intergenerational dialogue to mutually learn different generational views.

How can discussions within a group or with another demonstrate actions of change that tend to the needs of others? Encourage strategies that demonstrate utilize different contexts and needs

In what ways can you help unearth hidden messages from your subconscious to share and learn from others that are beyond a limited meaning and can demonstrate out-of-the-box possibilities?

If you allow yourself to focus on pauses and introspection, in what ways can you stimulate conversations that arise from a space between inductive and deductive reasoning? How would this be different from your experiences?

How can you have a give-and-take that allows you to thread information through the different contexts prevalent in your community? In what ways would new interconnections between different institutions create different mutual actions i.e., schools and law enforcement and senior living centers, etc.?

What directions can you explore that change toward an infinity of differences and not a specific goal?

How can a discussion based on mutual learning be open-ended to explore what occurs at the interface of how one context informs another context, and what differences would you expect?
